items.message: ok two things. my bank card got hit with a 30 day late back in 2024, it was a one time slip on my part, is there any way to get it taken off before my mortgage app? and if i sign up for the $6 credit builder and pay it like a week late one month, does that show up as a late on my report?
items.reply:
**1. Getting the 2024 late removed**

Since the late is accurate, it can legally stay on your report. No dispute or company can force it off early. Your profile shows a 30-day late on your Bank credit card, reported December 16, 2024. A late can stay for up to 7 years from the original missed payment, which was November 2024.

You can still send a goodwill letter. That's a short, polite note asking your card issuer to remove the late as a courtesy. It works best for a one-time slip on an otherwise clean account, which matches what you describe. The issuer doesn't have to agree, so treat it as a request, not a sure thing.

Even if it stays, its effect fades as it ages and on-time payments build up. Your card is current now, and your profile shows 4 months of on-time rent reported. Keeping every payment on time between now and your 2027 application helps the most.

**2. Paying the Credit Builder a week late**

A week late would not be reported as late. A payment 1 to 29 days past due isn't reported as late to the credit bureaus. Once it reaches 30 or more days past due, it is reported as late, which would hurt, especially close to a mortgage application.

For reference, the plan costs $6 a month for 24 months. Opening it needs no credit check or hard inquiry.

Next step: Write a short goodwill letter to your card issuer explaining the November 2024 slip and asking them to consider removing the late mark.

**1. Phone and electric bills**

Not by default. Many phone and utility companies don't report on-time payments to the credit bureaus themselves, so that history is often missing from reports.

The app has a free Bill Reporting feature. It looks for on-time utility, phone, and internet payments in your linked bank account and reports them to Equifax only, not Experian or TransUnion. Your profile shows Bill Reporting is not turned on. Your profile also doesn't say which bureau your VantageScore 3.0 of 641 comes from, so I can't say whether it would reflect these payments. A lender would also need to pull Equifax for them to count. Only on-time payments are reported, never late ones.

**2. Debt settlement on your auto loan**

No. Debt settlement only covers accounts that are charged off (written off by the lender as a loss) or in collections. Your profile shows your auto loan is open and current, with a $9,800 balance, so it doesn't qualify.

If you ever struggle with the payment, ask the lender about hardship options or talk with a nonprofit credit counselor. Settling would also not remove the account from your report or raise your score.

Keeping the auto loan current is what helps your mortgage plans. Your profile also shows one 30-day late payment on your bank credit card from 2024. If you think that is wrong, you can dispute it. If it's accurate, it can stay for its full reporting period, and steady on-time payments from here are what help.

Next step: Decide whether you want free Bill Reporting, and check which bureau your lender is likely to pull, since only Equifax would see those payments.

If anything in the letter looks wrong, you can request validation (proof of the debt) in writing.

**2. Will the charge-off disappear after settling?**

No. A settled account usually shows as "settled for less than the full balance," and it still shows as a charge-off. Settling doesn't shorten its 7-year reporting period. With a first missed payment in June 2024, it should drop off around June 2031.

There's no settlement yet. The fee is 20% of the amount saved, charged only after a deal is agreed and you make a payment. Forgiven debt may be taxable, so a tax professional can help with that. Get the terms in writing before you pay.
